blocks.text: 1. Chunk Overlap
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446842857-145192561.png
Chunk Overlap treats how much shared text between chunks actually helps as its own design decision.
It steps back from any one chunking strategy to examine overlap as its own dedicated design decision.
2. Overlap Revisited
Sliding windows, covered in Sliding Window Chunking, introduced overlap as a byproduct of how the window moves.
This topic treats overlap itself as the subject, independent of any single splitting method.
3. Overlap As A Percentage
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446842857-956186425.png
Overlap is most often expressed as a percentage of the chunk size, not a raw character count.
A ten percent overlap on a five hundred character chunk means fifty shared characters.

blocks.text: 4. Too Little Overlap
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446842858-441757873.png
As with the hard boundary problem in Sliding Window Chunking, too little overlap leaves boundary information stranded.
A reference or idea spanning a cut gets lost in neither neighboring chunk.
5. Too Much Overlap
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446843071-907485655.png
On the other end, too much overlap wastes storage on repeated content, the same cost of overlap tradeoff raised in Sliding Window Chunking.
Near duplicate chunks start crowding out diverse results during retrieval.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Excessive overlap produces chunks that are mostly repeated content with only a small unique portion, meaning a retrieval system can return several near identical results for what should have been one distinct match.

blocks.text: 6. Finding A Sensible Range
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446843071-858961375.png
Ten to twenty percent overlap serves as a common, practical starting range in real pipelines.
From that starting point, the value gets tuned based on actual retrieval results.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Starting at a moderate fifteen percent overlap and then observing whether retrieval quality improves or degrades as that number moves up or down is a practical, evidence driven way to tune this parameter.

blocks.text: 7. Overlap Intersects With Chunking Strategy
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446843072-599986990.png
Fixed chunking, covered in Fixed Chunking, benefits from overlap the most, since it ignores boundaries entirely.
Semantic or hierarchical chunking already respects boundaries, so it needs less overlap to compensate.

blocks.text: 8. Measuring Overlap Effectiveness
Comparing retrieval quality with and without overlap, an evaluation technique covered in a later module, reveals whether it is actually helping.
Overlap is a tunable parameter, not a fixed rule to apply blindly.
9. Recognizing How Much Overlap A Pipeline Actually Needs

blocks.alt: Recognizing How Much Overlap A Pipeline Actually Needs
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446843072-294109230.png
Fixed or lightly structured chunking benefits from meaningful overlap.
Boundary aware strategies like semantic or hierarchical chunking need only light or no overlap.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates computing overlap in characters from a percentage, and compares zero versus moderate overlap.

code.content:
document = (
    "Machine learning models require large amounts of training data to perform well. "
    "Without sufficient data, models tend to overfit and generalize poorly to new inputs."
)

def chunk_with_overlap(text, chunk_size, overlap_percent):
    # overlap expressed as a percentage of the chunk size
    overlap_chars = int(chunk_size * overlap_percent / 100)
    step = chunk_size - overlap_chars
    chunks = []
    start = 0
    while start < len(text):
        chunks.append(text[start:start + chunk_size])
        start += step
    return chunks

no_overlap = chunk_with_overlap(document, chunk_size=60, overlap_percent=0)
with_overlap = chunk_with_overlap(document, chunk_size=60, overlap_percent=15)

print("Zero overlap chunks:")
for c in no_overlap:
    print(f"  {c!r}")

print("\n15 percent overlap chunks:")
for c in with_overlap:
    print(f"  {c!r}")

print(f"\nOverlap in characters at 15 percent of a 60 character chunk: {int(60 * 0.15)}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the zero overlap chunks cutting cleanly with no shared text, while the overlap enabled chunks repeat a small tail of text at each boundary.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Setting overlap to zero regardless of chunking strategy, ignoring the hard boundary problem entirely.
Setting overlap so high that storage and near duplicate results become a real problem.
Using the same overlap percentage for every chunking strategy without considering how boundary aware each one already is.
Never measuring whether a given overlap setting actually improves retrieval quality.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Chunk overlap treats the amount of shared text between chunks as its own dedicated design decision.
Overlap is most often expressed as a percentage of the chunk size, not a raw character count.
Too little overlap leaves boundary information stranded between neighboring chunks.
Too much overlap wastes storage and can crowd out diverse results during retrieval.
Ten to twenty percent overlap is a common, practical starting range to tune from.
Fixed chunking benefits from overlap most; boundary aware strategies need less.
Comparing retrieval quality with and without overlap reveals whether it is actually helping.
Overlap is a tunable parameter, not a fixed rule to apply blindly to every pipeline.
